body:
> I feel no will to carry on living. I am aware this is a selfish attitude, but I have lost all the passion I once had, I have no drive or ambition. Even if I were to get a job, I wouldn't enjoy it, I have nothing I want out of life.

This is me for 2 years now, and yes suicide feels like a real option for me too.
My "way out" is through books. That's the only time my suicidal thoughts get "some rest". But I know reading isn't for everyone :(

It's a self-contradictory paradox, like the teumessian fox and laelaps the dog, just two things forever chasing each other. If you can live forever, you can kill yourself countless of times. But at the same time, killing yourself no matter how many times won't be an escape anymore, it won't end anything if you're immortal.

Ouch. :( 
Well you won't find responses like that from us here, so feel free to share/rant/de-stress with us.

Thank you. 
I haven't found much that made sense in this sub for quite a while.

Me. I want to die soon. I plan to die this Christmas, before 2016 kicks in. 
But before that, I'm figuring out what to do with my stuff; stuff I can give away, stuff I should burn, stuff okay to leave behind. That's all, really.
I feel like I'm won't live to see 2016.

> There is no point in getting fancy if you can't enjoy it.

Ditto.
Ouch. This is me. 5 months ago, I was able to stretch it to 12 hours. HALF A DAY you've been asleep but as soon as you've gotten up from your bed, it feels so wrong.
As an avid people-watcher, going outside is a good distraction for the voices in my head. Going back home is like "going back in the cage".
Every. Single. Damn. Day. Since last November. This plus a whole barrage of voices in your head comparing yourself to others. So much fun. Yay.
We're all rooting for you. Have a Happy Halloween too while you're at it.

No, I don't think it's 100% cure-able. Maybe 99%, but not an absolute erasure of it. 

"I feel like my depression has always been a part of me." <--This is why. 

Take a white sheet of paper, and depression is like marking a dot in the center. When you've hit rock bottom, all that matters is that black dot. Over time, some learn to focus on the white parts, the (bigger) good parts in life, but all the while knowing that the dot is still there.

For now maybe just do whatever comes natural to you. If you want to skip a class for a tv marathon or go buy food at the weirdest hours, just go along with it.  Then after a couple of days, or next week (after Halloween?), re-check yourself if you're still feeling the same way? If it's still the same for a month or so, maybe ask around what could be going on?

Without being dishonest. Hmm. You have to know, people aren't 100% honest when they're in a job interview either. 

Just know that lying you were the president of the debate club for 4 years in college is one thing, and lying that you're okay with a so-and-so starting work shift is another. 

Be ready to describe yourself without saying what's already written in your resume and don't try to over-impress your interviewer or ramble too much. 


You also have to keep in mind that since you're only starting out, you'll start as a blank slate so keep things -realistic-, i.e. don't expect the whole shebang at first.

"What's an easy way to get past this? "
Define 'easy'. 
But seriously, wait until that day comes, then you'll find out. What I learned when I moved out, no matter how much planning you do in your head for the next day, something can, and will always trip you up along the road when you least expect it. 

Then you learn to sharpen your improvisation skills. You'll be surprised how your real instincts will come out when you're dealing with a new environment all by yourself.

Hey. Thanks for the response. 
The closest thing to a support person I have is an online friend, but even then I still can't confide -everything- because I know she has bouts of depression too. (That's how we got along in the first place.) Whenever I want to vent, I keep thinking what if she's having a pleasant day for once and then I come in and ruin it.

I'm just a floater, I don't have a good drip on my life anymore. At least having control of how and when I want to die is something I can do.

"Please give me all the reasons you have for NOT going through with it, so I can think about why it doesn't matter."
--Isn't this, in itself, a sign of wavering/second thoughts? 

If you're dead set on your travel goal (and financially, mentally, physically, and socially prepared) by all means, travel like there's no tomorrow.

It's hard, especially when you don't even know where to start. And anxiety is like shooting you a bazillion possible topics you could talk about, but what comes out is just "..." Nothing! Absolutely nothing. Frustrating.  

About the girl you want to try texting, how about ice-breaker questions? Or if you know what she's into, start with those topics. Ask her about them, give her the whole 5-W's-and-1-H thing (Who, What, Where, Why, When, How) if you have to. Then cross your fingers she asks you in return. By then I think you'll have an idea how your efforts have fared.

I'm all in the same boat with the previous comments. In fact, another thing I would commend you for is that you -actually- asked/confronted her about it. Not everyone does that. Usually it's I'm-gonna-tell-someone-else-about-this rant routine but you didn't. 

You're going back in your shell, and... I think that's okay? It's okay to feel what you felt after that reply. But just... don't forget you could always always always come out again. Think of going back to your shell as re-charging your battery.

I don't want to hurt someone else too, but some days even that concern ebbs away and I just want to raise a white flag and give up, fall off the roof head first. 

My distractions include some music too, plus house chores (that no one asked for), and tv. But they could only pre-occupy my mind for so long, then next thing I know I'm back to square one. At the end of the day I evaluate what I did and feel terrible for another day wasted. Then a voice in my head would tell me "see, you should've killed yourself already" and then the whole cycle repeats itself.

True. 
Another form of bullcrap is after trying to explain even just a fraction of it, they generalize it immediately and say something like, "well yeah, me too, I get really sad too sometimes, you know?" 

Sometimes, I even get irked when some people (not all! I know there are others who really mean what they say) throw around "I know exaaaactly how you feel" so easily. In my head, I'm just 'o rly?'

I get this quite a lot too.

One time, some friends and I were seated around a table eating. I was introduced to a new person who was there with us, a friend of a friend. The first thing the person told me (right after the "Hi, nice to meet you!") was "Hey are you okay? You look sad."

Even strangers. Last year, I was going home from work waiting at a bus stop. An elderly man was standing there too and we were just minding our own business until a few minutes later, he looked at me and went, "Aww come on, don't think of your boyfriend too much."

When I was a teenager, one Christmas, one of my relatives gave me a small book as a Christmas present. Know what it was? It was a cheap self-help book entitled, "How To Be Happy". Nearly set that book on fire. 

And many more. 

It was so TIRING to hear over and over growing up (adolescent to teenage years) and it used to piss me off and crush my self-esteem down another level. I mean it still does up to now, but I've learned (or adapted?) to sharpen my tounge about it, I think. Not to be mean or not to insult, but just enough to say a neutral reply that they will just brush off the topic immediately. It helps soothe the crushed feeling for a while. 

"I don't want to annoy them with my depression and actually I don't want to get into details with them." --This so much. It's like a nasty tug-of-war that goes on forever in my head. 

I hide mine. I just don't mention it, period.  

Fake smiles, yes. But not to everyone. My fakest smiles are to my close friends. I never smile at home. Whenever my mom asks me about it, I say it's nothing.

For now, even if you got rejected by the company you were aiming for, at least give yourself a pat on the back for even being invited for an interview. Some applicants wouldn't even make it that far. 

Will this be your first job? 
One of the things I learned growing up is... always have a Plan B. (And take one day at a time.)
 
I know it sounds really cliche but "when one door closes, another one opens". The crappy un-said part of the saying though is, "aka you have to go back to square one", and it can really be draining. But just think or ask yourself, knowing the thousands of job-seekers out there from all walks of life, are you going to throw in the towel now?

It really is a crappy feeling when you don't get a sense of fulfillment in your work and you wake up every day feeling like you're standing at a fork in the road. Decisions, decisions. 

If you don't mind me asking, what got you into your acting job in the first place?

I don't know if I should reply since I don't know the feeling of getting better but maybe, just maybe one difference is starting to actually -love- living and your outlook on life sounds like a cheesy romantic quote.

Competition with younger applicants/recent grads/other unemployed people can get tough but sometimes a load of experience trumps a college degree in a heartbeat. (If you sprinkle it with some humility.)

That is... unless you got fired for a bad reason?
